lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- What Might Have Happened
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 17 -- What Might Have Happened
lesson.grammar_point: past modals of deduction (must have, might have, can't have)

listenings.text: I write detective novels, and readers often ask me where the clues come from. The honest answer is that I start at the end. I decide what really happened, and then I work backwards, leaving small things for the reader to find: a wet umbrella in a dry house, a train ticket in the wrong pocket. The best moment in any mystery is when the detective looks at those details and says: the gardener can't have done it, because he was in town all afternoon. Somebody must have opened the window from the inside. Readers love that moment, because it is exactly how we think in real life. We see a few facts and we fill in the gaps. The problem is that in real life we fill them in too quickly. My detective never jumps to conclusions. She writes down every explanation, even the far-fetched ones, and she only rules one out when a fact makes it impossible. That is why she is always right, and why I am usually wrong when I try to guess the ending of somebody else's book.

I am a forensic accountant, which means that when money disappears from a company, I am the person they call. Most people imagine the work is about finding a criminal. It is not. It is about building a timeline that nobody can argue with. In my first week on a case, I do not interview anyone. I follow the paper trail: invoices, bank records, emails, and the exact time each approval was made. People's memories are not reliable, but documents are. When I find a discrepancy, I write down every possible explanation. The invoice might have been entered twice by mistake. The manager might have approved it without reading it. Or somebody may have done it on purpose. Only after that do I talk to people, and I let them account for each gap in their own words. You would be surprised how often the explanation is innocent. In twenty years, I have learned one thing: the person who looks guilty on day one is usually not the one who did it.
